slides.content: Introduction Source (en) Unicorns bring joy to everyone they meet ↓ Target (nl) Eenhoorns brengen vreugde aan iedereen die ze ontmoeten Machine translation The task of translating text from a source language to a target language. 2 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Why is it useful? Information access • A lot of information on the web is in English • MT helps making it accessible to non-English speakers. 3 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Why is it useful? Computer-assisted translation (CAT) can speed up human translation. 4 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Why is it useful? Speech to speech translation can facilitate direct interaction. 5 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction Why is it useful? Translating images on the ﬂy can facilitate e.g. travelling. 6 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction What is diﬃcult? Word order Languages diﬀer in how they order words: E.g. the order of Subject (S) Verb (V) Object (O). English: He wrote a letter to a friend SVO Japanese: tomodachi ni tegami-o kaita (S)OV Friend to letter wrote Arabic: katabt ris¯ala li ˙sadq VSO wrote letter to friend 7 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction What is diﬃcult? Words in the source language do not always translate to the same word in the target language. En → Nl Bank bank oever (verb) indammen (verb) ophopen (See word sense disambiguation in lecture 9) 8 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction What is diﬃcult? Words in the source language do not always translate to the same word in the target language. En → Fr Dog chien chienne (Languages vary in morphology, see lecture 7) 8 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction What is diﬃcult? Languages may have lexical gaps wrt other languages. De → En Schadenfreude The joy a person feels from other people’s misfortune. Wanderlust The need to travel. etc. 9 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction What is diﬃcult? Some languages omit certain words. E.g. pro-drop languages omit certain pronouns. Spanish: Sofia llegó tarde porque ∅perdió el autobús. English: Sofia arrived late because she missed the bus. 10 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Supervised MT
slides.content: Supervised MT Machine translation requires training data: a parallel corpus. English Santa Claus teaches NLP to elves in the North Pole. They learn about machine translation and sentiment analysis. Santa loves training AI models for better toy recommendations. The elves code while enjoying hot cocoa and holiday cheer. Everyone prepares for a data-driven Christmas Eve delivery. Dutch De kerstman leert NLP aan elfen op de Noordpool. Ze leren over machinevertaling en sentimentanalyse. De Kerstman traint graag AI-modellen voor betere speelgoedaanbevelingen. De elfen programmeren terwijl ze genieten van warme chocolademelk en kerstsfeer. Iedereen bereidt zich voor op een datagestuurde kerstavondbezorging. 12 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Supervised MT
slides.content: Supervised MT It is not always that easy. Sample alignment of Le Petit Prince in English and French (Jurafsky and Martin, 2025) Not always a one-to-one mapping between sentences. 14 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Supervised MT
slides.content: Supervised MT Sentence alignment 1. Score pairs of spans to measure how likely they are to be translations • Using e.g. character lengths • Using a multilingual embedding space and cosine similarity 2. Align groups of up to 2 sentences based on these scores, using dynamic programming 15 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Supervised MT
slides.content: Supervised MT MT as a supervised task • Given a parallel corpus of sentences tokenized (into subwords) • Maximize the probability of the sequence of tokens in the target language y1, ..., ym, given the sequence of tokens in the source language x1, ..., xn: p(y1, ..., ym|x1, ..., xn) • Modelled via an encoder-decoder architecture: h = encoder(x) yt+1 = decoder(h, y1, ..., yt)∀t ∈[1, ..., m]) 16 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Decoding with Beam Search
slides.content: Decoding with Beam Search Greedy decoding • At each time step t, choose the highest probability word: ˆwt = arg max w∈V P(w|w1:t) • May lead to globally suboptimal choices →Beam search maintains multiple choices and leaves choice to later 24 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Decoding with Beam Search
slides.content: Decoding with Beam Search Beam search Search for the best path in a tree. Search tree for language modelling (Jurafsky and Martin, 2025) 25 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Decoding with Beam Search
slides.content: Decoding with Beam Search Beam search • Search for the best path in a tree. • Exhaustive search is too slow. • Instead, keep k possible tokens at each step • k is the beam width 26 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Decoding with Beam Search
slides.content: Decoding with Beam Search Beam search decoding with k = 2 (Jurafsky and Martin, 2025). 27 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Evaluation Evaluation dimensions Adequacy: How well the translation captures the exact meaning of the source sentence. Fluency: How ﬂuent the translation is in the target language (clarity, grammaticality) 29 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Human evaluation • Rating • Fluency • Adequacy: • How much information is preserved from source to target • Comparing to a reference translation • Ranking candidate translations • Post-edit the translation and measure the diﬀerence →Best evaluation but time consuming and expensive 30 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Automatic evaluation Comparison between a human reference translation and a candidate MT translation • chrF: character overlap • BLEU: word overlap • Embedding-based methods 31 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation chrF • Given a hypothesis candidate MT translation and a reference translation, • the character F-score measures the character overlap, • parametrized by k: the max length of the n-grams to consider. 33 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation chrF chrP: percentage of character 1-grams, 2-grams ... k-grams in the hypothesis that occur in the reference, averaged. chrR: percentage of character 1-grams, 2-grams ... k-grams in the reference that occur in the hypothesis, averaged. chrF+β: (1 + β2) chrP × chrR β2 × chrP + chrR chrF2: (common) 5 × chrP × chrR 4 × chrP + chrR 34 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation chrF example k = β = 2 REF witnessforthepast, unigrams: 18, bigrams: 17 HYP witnessofthepast, unigrams: 17, bigrams: 16 1-grams: 17 2-grams: 13 chrP: 1+.813 2 = .906 P 1-gram: 17 17 = 1 P 2-gram: 13 16 = .813 note: the comma is counted as a character 35 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation chrF example k = β = 2 REF witnessforthepast, unigrams: 18, bigrams: 17 HYP witnessofthepast, unigrams: 17, bigrams: 16 1-grams: 17 2-grams: 13 chrP: 1+.813 2 = .906 chrR: .944+.765 2 = .855 R 1-gram: 17 18 = .944 R 2-gram: 13 17 = .765 35 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation chrF example k = β = 2 REF witnessforthepast, unigrams: 18, bigrams: 17 HYP witnessofthepast, unigrams: 17, bigrams: 16 1-grams: 17 2-grams: 13 chrP: 1+.813 2 = .906 chrR: .944+.765 2 = .855 chrF: 5 chrP×chrP 4chrP+chrR = .86 35 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation BLEU • Based on overlap of word n-grams • Using precision only: • Percentage of word 1-grams, 2-grams, 3-grams and 4-grams in the hypothesis that occur in the reference. • This is calculated across all the sentences of the corpus. • Using a brevity penalty: • penalizing translations that are too short • Note: sensitive to word tokenization! 36 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Illustration of n−gram overlap accuracies as part of computing BLEU. Image by Dan Klein . 37 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Limitations of chrF and BLEU • Synonymy (or more generally, word meaning) is not captured (see lecture 9) • Word order diﬀerences are not captured • Cross-sentence properties are not captured (e.g. discourse coherence, see lecture 10). • Generally, highly criticized but still heavily used for lack of (cheap) alternatives 38 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation Embedding-based evaluation • Given a hypothesis translation, a reference translation and a rating • Fine-tune an encoder to predict the rating • Given a hypothesis translation, a reference translation: • Compute embeddings of the hypothesis and the reference using an encoder • Measure the similarity of the embeddings 40 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.content: Evaluation BertScore visualization (Jurafsky and Martin, 2025). R : average max similarity per reference word P : average max similarity per candidate word 41 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges SOTA Quality tiers Publishable: Publish as is HTER: 0-10% Editable: Requires post-editing HTER: 10-20% Gistable: Useful for information gathering or trend spotting HTER: 20-40% Triagable: Only useful for identifying relevant documents HTER: 40-50% Tiers deﬁned based on human-annotator translation editor rate (HTER). The scale was developed in preparation of the DARPA GALE programme. 44 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges SOTA Language pairs and domains assessment French-English restricted domain publishable French-English news stories publishable German-English news stories publishable Swahili-English news stories gistable Uyghur-English news stories triagable Informal estimates by Philipp Koehn. 45 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges • MT relies on large parallel corpora • Only available for a fraction of possible language pairs • What can we do in low-resource settings? 47 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Backtranslation A type of data augmentation to add sentence pairs to the training data. 48 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Multilingual models One model, many translation directions. Illustration of a many-to-many machine translation model (Aharoni et al., 2019). 49 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Multilingual models • One model for 100s of language pairs (Aharoni et al., 2019). • Enables cross-lingual transfer between related languages (e.g. Spanish and Catalan). • Empirically performs competitively for some language pairs. 50 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Low-resource MT Limitations and open challenges • Low-resource MT is still very much an open challenge • NMT models are data hungry • Certain language properties make MT more diﬃcult: • Morphological complexity (e.g. Ataman and Federico (2018)) • Word order freedom (Bisazza et al., 2021) • Data quality can be an issue (Kreutzer et al., 2022) • English almost always included in language pairs under study 51 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Low-resource MT Limitations and open challenges AmericasNLP shared task (De Gibert et al., 2025) involving polysynthetic languages: • Poor baselines, hard to beat • LLMs help if target side is high-resource, otherwise not. 52 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Some languages encode grammatical gender (Spanish, Italian, Russian, ...) Others do not (English, Turkish, Basque, Finnish) 54 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges In some cases, this can lead to two possible translations. En The doctor asked for help. ↓ Es La doctora pidió ayuda. El doctor pidió ayuda. 55 NLP: Machine translation

slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Results on gender translation accuracy. 63 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges • Gender bias in MT is still an open challenge. • There are some methods to mitigate it, e.g. using controlled text generation (Lu et al., 2023). • There is a workshop dedicated to this, Gender Inclusive Translation Technologies GITT. 64 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: SOTA and open challenges
slides.content: SOTA and open challenges Open challenges • Low-resource MT • Gender bias • Document-level translation (Läubli et al., 2018) • Eﬃcient improvements over beam search • Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) is computationally expensive (Trabelsi et al., 2024) • Low-frequency words • Out-of-domain data See also Koehn and Knowles (2017), still largely relevant today. 66 NLP: Machine translation

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary Summary • Machine translation with a neural encoder-decoder model • Decoding with beam search • Automatic evaluation methods and their limitations • State-of-the art: highly dependent on language pairs and domain • Strategies for low-resource MT • Gender bias in MT • Overall, much progress but big open challenges 68 NLP: Machine translation
